title: Arjuna joins his palms
hook: before God's universal form, Arjuna joins his palms; at an arrivals gate, a grandmother does the same
carry: anjali: one bow for God, elders and guests
tomorrow: Why does Shiva teach without a word?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seals that wake the goddess within: the body as the place where Shiva and Shakti meet.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `THE SEALS THAT WAKE THE GODDESS WITHIN.`

segments.voice: The arrivals gate at an airport, late in the evening. A tired young man comes through the sliding doors pulling a suitcase. An older woman at the rail sees him, and before she hugs him, before she says his name, she presses her palms together in front of her chest and dips her head. He does it back. Then the hug. Two seconds, maybe less, and nobody around them notices. That small shape of the hands is a mudra, so familiar it's easy to forget it is one.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS GATE, LATE.` → `PALMS TOGETHER, A DIP OF THE HEAD.` → `A MUDRA, HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: The gesture has a name: anjali. Two palms joined, fingers pointing up, usually held at the chest, sometimes at the forehead. Anjali can also mean the cupped hollow of two hands, the shape you'd make to carry water or flowers as an offering. So the joined palms carry a sense of offering. And namaste? That's not the gesture. It's the words said with it: namas, a bow; te, to you. Now watch the Bhagavad Gita use this mudra at its most overwhelming moment. In chapter eleven, Arjuna has been given the divine eye and sees Krishna's universal form, vast, blazing, with many faces and eyes. The text tells us what his body does. In paraphrase: filled with wonder, his hair standing on end, Arjuna bowed his head, joined his palms, and spoke. Later, trembling, palms still joined, he bows again and speaks in a choking voice, bowing to Krishna in front, behind, on every side. Notice what the text shows first. Not Arjuna's thoughts. His hands. Before God, the hands go first. And here's the teaching that carries that bow off the battlefield. The Taittiriya Upanishad sends its students home with a list, in paraphrase: let your mother be a god to you, your father a god, your teacher a god, your guest a god. That's why the same joined palms greet the murti in the shrine and the grandmother at the door. In this teaching, the divine is honored in the people in front of you, and anjali is how the hands say it.
screen: `ANJALI: PALMS JOINED, AN OFFERING.` · `NAMASTE: THE WORDS. A BOW TO YOU.` · `ARJUNA, AMAZED, JOINS HIS PALMS.` · `MOTHER, FATHER, TEACHER, GUEST: AS GOD.` · then, large: `ONE BOW, FOR GOD AND FOR NANI.`

segments.voice: Bring the palms together in front of the chest, fingers pointing up, thumbs resting lightly near the breastbone, and let the head dip a little. Bring to mind an elder, a teacher or a guest, and hold the gesture toward them for a few breaths, as the Upanishad says: as you would toward God. If you pray, offer the same bow to the deity you love. If the arms tire, let the hands rest in the lap and keep the feeling.
The mudras. Today, anjali: two palms joined in offering, the same bow for God, for elders and for guests.
Your line: anjali: one bow for God, elders and guests. Tomorrow, a teacher who says nothing at all. Go gently.
